high_cited.venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control

high_cited.title: Bridging the Gap between Optimal Trajectory Planning and Safety-Critical Control with Applications to Autonomous Vehicles
high_cited.abstract: We address the problem of optimizing the performance of a dynamic system while satisfying hard safety constraints at all times. Implementing an optimal control solution is limited by the computational cost required to derive it in real time, especially when constraints become active, as well as the need to rely on simple linear dynamics, simple objective functions, and ignoring noise. The recently proposed Control Barrier Function (CBF) method may be used for safety-critical control at the expense of sub-optimal performance. In this paper, we develop a real-time control framework that combines optimal trajectories generated through optimal control with the computationally efficient CBF method providing safety guarantees. We use Hamiltonian analysis to obtain a tractable optimal solution for a linear or linearized system, then employ High Order CBFs (HOCBFs) and Control Lyapunov Functions (CLFs) to account for constraints with arbitrary relative degrees and to track the optimal state, respectively. We further show how to deal with noise in arbitrary relative degree systems. The proposed framework is then applied to the optimal traffic merging problem for Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) where the objective is to jointly minimize the travel time and energy consumption of each CAV subject to speed, acceleration, and speed-dependent safety constraints. In addition, when considering more complex objective functions, nonlinear dynamics and passenger comfort requirements for which analytical optimal control solutions are unavailable, we adapt the HOCBF method to such problems. Simulation examples are included to compare the performance of the proposed framework to optimal solutions (when available) and to a baseline provided by human-driven vehicles with results showing significant improvements in all metrics.

high_cited.title: Safety-Critical Control using Optimal-decay Control Barrier Function with Guaranteed Point-wise Feasibility
high_cited.abstract: Safety is one of the fundamental problems in robotics. Recently, a quadratic program based control barrier function (CBF) method has emerged as a way to enforce safety-critical constraints. Together with control Lyapunov function (CLF), it forms a safety-critical control strategy, named CLF-CBF-QP, which can mediate between achieving the control objective and ensuring safety, while being executable in real-time. However, once additional constraints such as input constraints are introduced, the CLF-CBF-QP may encounter infeasibility. In order to address the challenge arises due to the infeasibility, we propose an optimal-decay form for safety-critical control wherein the decay rate of the CBF is optimized point-wise in time so as to guarantee point-wise feasibility when the state lies inside the safe set. The proposed control design is numerically validated using an adaptive cruise control example.

high_cited.title: Rule-Based Safety-Critical Control Design using Control Barrier Functions with Application to Autonomous Lane Change
high_cited.abstract: This paper develops a new control design for guaranteeing a vehicle's safety during lane change maneuvers in a complex traffic environment. The proposed method uses a finite state machine (FSM), where a quadratic program based optimization problem using control Lyapunov functions and control barrier functions (CLF-CBF-QP) is used to calculate the system's optimal inputs via rule-based control strategies. The FSM can make switches between different states automatically according to the command of driver and traffic environment, which makes the ego vehicle find a safe opportunity to do a collision-free lane change maneuver. By using a convex quadratic program, the controller can guarantee the system's safety at a high update frequency. A set of pre-designed typical lane change scenarios as well as randomly generated driving scenarios are simulated to show the performance of our controller.

high_cited.title: Pointwise Feasibility of Gaussian Process-based Safety-Critical Control under Model Uncertainty
high_cited.abstract: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and Control Lyapunov Functions (CLFs) are popular tools for enforcing safety and stability of a controlled system, respectively. They are commonly utilized to build constraints that can be incorpo-rated in a min-norm quadratic program (CBF-CLF-QP) which solves for a safety-critical control input. However, since these constraints rely on a model of the system, when this model is inaccurate the guarantees of safety and stability can be easily lost. In this paper, we present a Gaussian Process (GP)-based approach to tackle the problem of model uncertainty in safety-critical controllers that use CBFs and CLFs. The considered model uncertainty is affected by both state and control input. We derive probabilistic bounds on the effects that such model uncertainty has on the dynamics of the CBF and CLF. We then use these bounds to build safety and stability chance constraints that can be incorporated in a min-norm convex optimization-based controller, called GP-CBF-CLF-SOCP. As the main theoretical result of the paper, we present necessary and sufficient conditions for pointwise feasibility of the proposed optimization problem. We believe that these conditions could serve as a starting point towards understanding what are the minimal requirements on the distribution of data collected from the real system in order to guarantee safety. Finally, we validate the proposed framework with numerical simulations of an adaptive cruise controller for an automotive system.
high_cited.journal: 2021 60th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
high_cited.venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control

high_cited.title: Safety-critical Control with Nonaffine Control Inputs via a Relaxed Control Barrier Function for an Autonomous Vehicle
high_cited.abstract: When designing a controller for the autonomous vehicle system, safety and trajectory tracking performance are two major concerns. This letter proposes a novel control design for an autonomous vehicle system with nonaffine control inputs that can track the desired trajectories while considering the safety constraint. First, the vehicle dynamics is modeled using the differential flatness approach. The dynamic inversion method is then employed for the trajectory tracking of a nonaffine-in control system, and a control barrier function (CBF) approach is utilized to enforce the safety constraint. The trajectory tracking control is handled as a least-squares optimization problem, while the CBF is considered as a constraint. By relaxing the CBF constraint to the cost function, the novel control design is derived via a dynamic inversion. The safety and the stability of the closed-loop system are analyzed using a singular perturbation method. The proposed method is validated using the numerical simulation and the high-fidelity car simulator under realistic driving scenarios.

high_cited.title: Data-Driven Safety-Critical Control: Synthesizing Control Barrier Functions with Koopman Operators
high_cited.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a powerful tool to guarantee safety of autonomous systems, yet they rely on the computation of control invariant sets, which is notoriously difficult. A backup strategy employs an implicit control invariant set computed by forward integrating the system dynamics. However, this integration is prohibitively expensive for high dimensional systems, and inaccurate in the presence of unmodelled dynamics. We propose to learn discrete-time Koopman operators of the closed-loop dynamics under a backup strategy. This approach replaces forward integration by a simple matrix multiplication, which can mostly be computed offline. We also derive an error bound on the unmodeled dynamics in order to robustify the CBF controller. Our approach extends to multi-agent systems, and we demonstrate the method on collision avoidance for wheeled robots and quadrotors.

high_cited.title: Predictive Control Barrier Functions for Online Safety Critical Control
high_cited.abstract: This paper presents a methodology for constructing Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) that proactively consider the future safety of a system along a nominal trajectory, and effect corrective action before the trajectory leaves a designated safe set. Specifically, this paper presents a systematic approach for propagating a nominal trajectory on a receding horizon, and then encoding the future safety of this trajectory into a CBF. If the propagated trajectory is unsafe, then a controller satisfying the CBF condition will modify the nominal trajectory before the trajectory becomes unsafe. Compared to existing CBF techniques, this strategy is proactive rather than reactive and thus potentially results in smaller modifications to the nominal trajectory. The proposed strategy is shown to be provably safe, and then is demonstrated in simulated scenarios where it would otherwise be difficult to construct a traditional CBF. In simulation, the predictive CBF results in less modification to the nominal trajectory and smaller control inputs than a traditional CBF, and faster computations than a nonlinear model predictive control approach.
high_cited.journal: 2022 IEEE 61st Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
high_cited.venue: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control

high_cited.title: Safety-Critical Path Planning for Obstacle Avoidance Based on Reinforcement Learning and Control Barrier Functions
high_cited.abstract: This article presents a safety-critical control framework for navigation in complex environments with numerous obstacles. An online robust path planning scheme is developed by integrating reinforcement learning (RL) with control barrier functions (CBFs). First, a disturbance observer is designed to estimate the unknown disturbance along with a derived upper bound of the estimation error. Then, a nominal controller is designed using RL, where a critic neural network (NN) structure is established by using state-following (StaF) kernel function. Additionally, by employing a state extrapolation technique, the learning process leverages both real-time and simulated experience data. To ensure safety, obstacle avoidance is formulated as a forward invariance problem of safe sets defined by CBFs. Subsequently, the CBF-based safety-critical constraints are integrated into a quadratic programming (QP) framework to modify the nominal controller. Furthermore, these CBFs are incorporated into a composite CBF using smooth approximation, enabling efficient constraint consolidation. Then, an explicit safe control policy is proposed that guarantees collision-free path planning. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed scheme is demonstrated through numerical simulations, and comparative results show the advantages over the existing methods in motion trajectory.

high_cited.title: Learning Differentiable Safety-Critical Control using Control Barrier Functions for Generalization to Novel Environments
high_cited.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have become a popular tool to enforce safety of a control system. CBFs are commonly utilized in a quadratic program formulation (CBF-QP) as safety-critical constraints. A class $\mathcal{K}$ function in CBFs usually needs to be tuned manually in order to balance the trade-off between performance and safety for each environment. However, this process is often heuristic and can become intractable for high relative-degree systems. Moreover, it prevents the CBF-QP from generalizing to different envi-ronments in the real world. By embedding the optimization procedure of the exponential control barrier function based quadratic program (ECBF-QP) as a differentiable layer within a deep learning architecture, we propose a differentiable safety-critical control framework that enables generalization to new environments for high relative-degree systems with forward invariance guarantees. Finally, we validate the proposed control design with 2D double and quadruple integrator systems in various environments.

arxiv.title: From Local to Global: Sheaf-Theoretic Control Barrier Functions on Manifolds
arxiv.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide formal safety guarantees for dynamical systems by rendering a safe set forward-invariant via pointwise-optimal feedback control. While the CBF framework is well established for dynamical systems in Euclidean space, there exist gaps for systems evolving on non-Euclidean manifolds. For systems modeled as constrained control differential inclusions, we introduce the Sheaf-CBF: a sheaf-theoretic framework for CBFs on smooth manifolds and vector bundles. The differential inclusions are formulated intrinsically on the control bundle, and analogous regularity properties in the Euclidean case are established fiberwise under local trivializations. Regularity conditions are given under which a pointwise-optimal feedback law is single-valued and continuous over local charts. Framed as a local-to-global optimization problem, sheaf-theoretic restriction and gluing compatibility conditions on overlapping charts are shown to uniquely determine a continuous global section of the control bundle, thereby guaranteeing forward invariance of the safe set. Numerical simulations on a nontrivial M{ö}bius strip demonstrate that failure of sheaf compatibility results in violations of safety, whereas the Sheaf-CBF maintains forward invariance.

arxiv.title: Safety of layered control systems via control barrier morphisms
arxiv.abstract: Layered control architectures provide a powerful paradigm for synthesizing controllers for complex systems. Yet, translating guarantees at each layer to system-level guarantees is challenging due to the interactions between layers. To address this problem, this paper presents a categorical perspective on layered control architectures. Individual systems are represented as control coalgebras, their interactions are specified as morphisms to mediators, and system-level behaviors are obtained via composition defined categorically as a pullback. To analyze the safety of these systems, we formulate control barrier morphisms (CBMs), the categorical generalization of control barrier functions. We prove that feedback controllers satisfying a CBM condition render the associated safe subobject forward invariant. It is through CBMs that we can establish the safety of layered systems: given a CBM at each layer subject to compatibility conditions, the universal property of the pullback implies the existence of a CBM for the composed system. Safety of a full-order model being safety filtered by a reduced-order model is recovered as a specialization of the categorical framework.

arxiv.title: Robust Dynamic Safety Margins are Robust Control Barrier Functions
arxiv.abstract: This paper establishes robustness properties for control barrier functions (CBFs) constructed using dynamic safety margins (DSMs). We show that DSMs can act as robust CBFs by leveraging input-to-state stability for Lyapunov-based constructions, and contractivity for trajectory-prediction-based approaches. Additionally, we derive closed-form DSM-based robust CBFs (RDSM-RCBFs) specifically for linear systems. Simulations highlight the improved robustness of the proposed RDSM-RCBFs compared to nominal DSM-CBF baselines.

arxiv.title: Localization-Uncertainty-Aware UAV Swarm Search for GNSS-Denied Maritime Surveillance
arxiv.abstract: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices. First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain. Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds. Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended Kalman filter in the loop. The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs. An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5 s, 20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible and containment in at least 98.97% of UAV-frames, and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence. The source code is publicly available.

arxiv.title: SCET-CBF: Speed-Calibrated Soft Guidance for One-Step Dynamic Navigation
arxiv.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) support collision avoidance, yet dense dynamic encounters can leave a vehicle with no feasible command. Geometric refinements and soft constraints help preserve motion choices. Using these choices also requires accounting for the vehicle's changing turning response. For a steering-limited bicycle, braking can lower closing speed while slowing the lateral motion needed before an obstacle arrives. We propose SCET-CBF, a speed-calibrated soft guidance law for one-step dynamic navigation. A short lateral escape maneuver gives an allowable approach speed. Its speed derivative allows a quadratic program to weigh both effects of braking when choosing acceleration and steering. Soft penalties accommodate competing obstacle preferences within the input set permitted by segment and braking constraints. We derive the guidance and establish protection over each accepted motion segment, together with conditional braking invariance for a single obstacle. On 2500 paired tasks with a 60 s deadline, SCET achieves 72.8% completion, compared with 49.8% for CBF/velocity-obstacle control and 69.8% for an enhanced 1 s CBF-MPC. At 100 obstacles, SCET and the enhanced MPC complete 52.4% and 33.6% of tasks. Paired studies identify the contributions of speed feedback and early activation. Further evaluations examine the operating range under lateral acceleration limits and bounded motion and execution errors.

arxiv.title: History-Aware Control Barrier Functionals with Nonsingular Fading-Memory Kernels
arxiv.abstract: Safety-critical protection often depends not only on the state and physical limits of the system, but on how that state evolved over time. Here, the safety margin measures the remaining allowance before a physical limit is reached. In this context, the objective is to enforce both physical safety and history-dependent retention of this margin for integer-order control-affine systems. To this end, changes in this margin are converted into memory through fading-memory kernels with finite nonnegative weights. A history-aware control barrier functional (HA-CBFal) is constructed explicitly, with nonnegativity equivalent to retaining a prescribed fraction of this margin's weighted historical value. This condition is enforced by an affine input constraint and proved to imply physical safety under stated kernel, initialization, and feasibility conditions, without finite-dimensional memory realization. In 36 calibration cases on the ADMIRE flight-control benchmark, mean per-case tracking-RMSE reductions of 27.2\% and 7.0\% are obtained relative to calibrated state-only CBF and moving-average control barrier functional (MA-CBFal), respectively, with both constraints preserved to numerical tolerance. In a shorter-recovery maneuver outside calibration with frozen gains, both constraints are preserved to tolerance by HA-CBFal and state-only CBF, but the retention requirement is violated despite MA-CBFal nonnegativity.

arxiv.title: Using Finite-Time Control to Synthesize Dynamic Backup Control Barrier Functions
arxiv.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for the construction of control barrier functions (CBFs) for controllable linear systems subject to multiple state and input constraints. The approach is based on the Dynamic Backup CBF (DB-CBF) framework, where the control policy is parametrized using the equilibrium subspace of the system. By using a minimum-energy finite-time controller, we show that the terminal set constraint trivially reduces to having an admissible equilibrium point. The proposed DB-CBF is easy to tune (one parameter), fully takes advantage of the input range (by minimizing the control effort), and guarantees constraint enforcement (by tracking a backup equilibrium point that can be reached safely in finite time).

arxiv.title: SAFTER: Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability for Robust Reinforcement Learning under Distribution Shift
arxiv.abstract: Learning safe policies that generalize to unseen environments is difficult under bounded actuation, where an unsafe decision may become unrecoverable. Conventional control barrier function (CBF) filters enforce only instantaneous safety and ignore future recoverability. We propose SAFTER (Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability), which embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter into Soft Actor-Critic training. SAFTER unifies current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input admissibility into a single differentiable certificate. Its CBF condition yields an exact minimum-intervention projection without iterative online optimization. In quadruped navigation, SAFTER reaches 90% training success with 30.6% fewer transitions than Vanilla SAC and 34.1-35.1% fewer than current-state CBF-filtered SAC baselines. Across unseen simulated environments, SAFTER improves success by up to 42.4 and 61.4 percentage points over the state-of-the-art methods CBF-RL and SEA-Nav, respectively, and achieves 73.3% and 76.7% success on two real-world navigation maps. Ablations identify accurate differentiation through the safety filter as a key contributor to robustness, in which replacing the projection Jacobian with the identity approximation reduces success rate in a High-Shift environment from 61.4% to 6.2%. These results show that recoverability-aware filtering serves as both a runtime safety mechanism and a learning mechanism for sample-efficient, robust policies.

arxiv.title: Prescribed Performance Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning for Roundabout Navigation of Autonomous Vehicles
arxiv.abstract: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) face significant challenges in roundabout navigation due to dense traffic interactions and unpredictable agent behaviors, necessitating high levels of adaptability and safety. While the combination of Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a promising approach, existing frameworks suffer from a structural mismatch where pointwise RL decisions fail to align with MPC's trajectory level optimization, and often lack rigorous safety guarantees. This work proposes RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF, a hierarchical framework for safe, smooth and comfort roundabout navigation, which regulates the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control. We employ Prescribed Performance Constraints (PPC) to enforce a gradual, stable convergence between reference trajectories and control outputs, ensuring MPC tracking performance remains consistent with intended behavior from RL. Additionally, a Control Barrier Function (CBF) layer provides real-time safety corrections that are fed back into the RL process. Simulation results in the MetaDrive environment demonstrate that our method achieves a 6.25\% increase in average success rate and a 65.87\% reduction in Motion Sickness Dose Value (MSDV) compared to the optimal baseline, meanwhile accelerating training convergence.

arxiv.title: Safe Barrier Function Control for Grid-Following Inverters under Weak Grid Conditions
arxiv.abstract: This paper proposes a barrier control approach for the safe regulation of grid-following voltage-source-converters (VSC), operating in weak grid conditions. The proposed controller aims to enhance the transient performance and synchronization properties of the VSC, providing frequency and current limiting guarantees by employing smooth control barrier functions. First, a dynamic model is derived that includes the dynamic state interactions that are omitted in quasi-steady-state approaches, revealing the destabilizing elements both during transient and steady-state performance. Then, it is analytically proven that the proposed control law guarantees frequency limitation and inner current evolution in prescribed safety regions, while counteracting the destabilizing strong coupling between PCC voltage and injected current. In addition, sufficient conditions are formulated that guarantee the stability of the closed-loop system with respect to desired operating points. The theoretic results are verified in simulations of case studies operating in varying grid strength.

arxiv.title: Lifting Safety Through Reduced-Order Model Architectures: An Invariant Manifold Approach
arxiv.abstract: Reduced-order model architectures are often used to decompose complex safety-critical control design tasks into tractable subproblems. In this paradigm, one must ask: when does the safety of a reduced-order model lift to safety of the full system? Taking an invariant manifold perspective, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of smooth, regular lifts of compact safe sets from reduced-order models. Our characterization relies only on asymptotic stability of an embedding of a reduced-order safe set, without additional robustness or rate conditions. We apply these results to study control barrier functions in reduced-order model architectures and lifts of safe sets through cascades. Further, we use our conditions to obtain topological obstructions to the tracking of safe, kinematic reduced-order models for mechanical systems. We conclude by using these obstructions to inform safe hierarchical control design for an underactuated satellite on SE(3).

arxiv.title: TrajEdit: Real-Time Flow-Matching Trajectory Adaptation via FlowEdit and CBF Safety Filter
arxiv.abstract: Safe, real-time motion planning is especially difficult when a dynamic obstacle actively pursues the ego agent, requiring rapid adaptation as the environment changes. We present TrajEdit, a hierarchical trajectory planner for pursuit-evasion that combines flow matching, trajectory editing, and safety filtering. Rather than regenerating trajectories from scratch at every step, TrajEdit follows the current plan under nominal conditions and adapts its remaining portion through FlowEdit as the pursuer approaches, and falls back to a control barrier function safety filter if the adversarial agent is within a safety threshold. Our use of FlowEdit for trajectory editing reduces computation time while maintaining a comparable success rate. We evaluate TrajEdit in 2D pursuit-evasion with static obstacles and an adversarial pursuer, demonstrating high success rates with low capture and collision rates, while achieving computational time savings over full replanning baselines.

arxiv.title: FLASH-CBF-RRT: Fast Lipschitz-Adaptive Safe Horizon CBF Steering for Certified Motion Planning
arxiv.abstract: Fast motion planning requires both sample-efficient exploration and computationally efficient local steering. Conventional straight-line steering is inexpensive but wastes samples by rejecting colliding extensions. Quadratic program controllers with control barrier function (CBF) constraints can be used to achieve effective local steering but can increase the planning time due to the expensive sequential evaluations. We develop a method to accelerate CBF steering by computing a time horizon within which CBF-filtered velocity may be applied constantly using closed-form kinematic bounds on collision-clearance. Our method, FLASH-CBF-RRT, significantly reduces the number of evaluations compared to prior CBF-RRT approaches because the planner can take adaptive steering step sizes that are shorter near obstacles and longer in open space. We implement this steering procedure as an extension of RRT-Connect in OMPL. Across 689 MotionBenchMaker problems, FLASH-CBF-RRT matches RRT-Connect's 100% success rate while reducing median planning time by 3.82x, and is 3.88x faster than fixed-step CBF-RRT. Hardware experiments on a 17-DoF mobile manipulator demonstrate 2.2x faster planning and 4.2x fewer evaluations. Videos and results are available at: https://mamani828.github.io/FLASH-CBF-RRT/.

arxiv.title: Anytime-Valid Certification of Robustness Margins for Safe Control via E-Values
arxiv.abstract: Robust control uses the error between a known model and the true system as a robustness margin. However, this error is usually unknown: conservative estimates restrict feasibility and performance, while underestimates can result in violations of the control property. We estimate this robustness margin from online data using e-values, a statistical tool for hypothesis testing, in the setting of discrete-time control barrier functions (CBFs). Here, we measure the robustness margin as the difference between the observed CBF and the model-based CBF prediction. We then design a robust CBF controller in three steps by: (1) selecting a set of candidate margins, (2) obtaining validity certificates for these candidates via sequential tests based on e-values, and (3) updating the CBF controller with the smallest certified candidate. The deployed tests accumulate evidence against the hypothesis that an exceedance risk, the probability of the robustness margin exceeding the candidate margin, remains at or above a pre-specified failure probability $α$. Our tests are anytime valid and thus enable the use of certified candidates in the CBF controller, guaranteeing that the probability that the exceedance risk of a certified margin exceeds $α$ is at most a user-chosen confidence $δ$. We validate our approach on navigation problems across different environments with visualizations in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

arxiv.title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions
arxiv.abstract: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.

arxiv.title: CBF-Based Control Allocation for Omnidirectional Tiltrotor Aerial Robots
arxiv.abstract: Actively tilting aerial robots can generate six-dimensional wrenches, but slow servo response can make a desired wrench infeasible during reconfiguration. This paper develops a control barrier function (CBF) allocator that preserves wrench feasibility under bounded servo-configuration mismatch. An exact equivalent-wrench identity connects the thrust required at nominal and actual configurations. For a nonsingular six-channel allocation map, inverse allocation reduces robust wrench containment to twelve thrust margins tightened by an ellipsoidal reserve. Their complete derivatives yield a six-variable servo-rate quadratic program, followed by differential thrust allocation for tracking. A conditional forward-invariance result establishes actual-configuration feasibility under reserve coverage, feasible initialization, and admissible CBF inputs. A complementary MuJoCo study evaluates a measured-angle implementation against geometric, augmented differential, and normalized differential allocation in circular and cartwheel maneuvers, with and without disturbances. The proposed implementation achieves lower position error in all four recorded scenarios, with an attitude tradeoff in circular tracking. During the disturbed cartwheel, the desired wrench is feasible at all 1751 stored samples of continuous rotation; baseline violation rates range from 60.8% to 100%. These comparisons evaluate sampled feasibility; validation of the nominal-trajectory certificate requires nominal-state and reserve-coverage records.

arxiv.title: From Optical Flow to Safety: Visual Safety Certification via Scale-Free Relative Motion
arxiv.abstract: Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF). An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.

arxiv.title: Regions of Attraction of CBF-Based Safety Filters for Stable Planar Linear Systems
arxiv.abstract: In this paper we study the dynamical properties induced by safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs). These are obtained by minimally modifying a nominal controller with the goal of rendering it safe. We consider the simple setting of a planar linear plant with a stable linear nominal controller and an affine constraint. We show that even in this simple setting, the filtered system can oscillate or diverge while remaining safe. We fully characterize the parameters for which the origin is globally (exponentially or asymptotically) stable. For all other parameters, the filter creates a saddle on the constraint boundary, and we characterize the region of attraction of the origin. For underdamped nominal dynamics, its boundary is an unstable periodic orbit, a homoclinic loop, or the saddle's stable manifold, depending on whether the CBF gain is below, at, or above a homoclinic transition value. A vehicle sideslip example and two three-dimensional examples illustrate the results and what changes beyond planar dynamics.

arxiv.title: BubbleCBF: Constructive Safety for Second-Order Systems and Application to Autonomous Robot Navigation in Unknown Environments
arxiv.abstract: Satisfying safety constraints for systems with second-order dynamics is challenging because a position constraint may require infeasible deceleration. Higher-order control barrier functions (CBFs) provide an approach for expressing safety conditions for such systems but feasibility depends on the system dynamics and available control authority. We develop a constructive approach for designing feasible safety constraints for second-order control-affine systems. Starting from a signed distance function (SDF), we construct collision-free spheres, i.e., bubbles, in position space, and use their quadratic geometry and overlap to construct a velocity-dependent safety constraint. The associated safe set is represented as a union of intersections and enforced through a quadratic-program safety filter. Under mild assumptions on the dynamics, bubble overlap, and design parameters, we prove that the quadratic-program-based controller is well defined, continuous in the system state, and renders the set forward invariant. We also derive sufficient conditions for feasibility under bounded inputs. We demonstrate that our BubbleCBF, applied to a differential-drive robot, achieves safe autonomous navigation in unknown environments. Videos and results are available at: https://existentialrobotics.org/bubblecbf/.

arxiv.title: Optimal Decay Matrix Control Barrier Functions: Soundness and Completeness for Matrix Safety Constraints
arxiv.abstract: Many safety requirements, such as keeping a manipulator away from kinematic singularities, a network connected, or a system observable, amount to keeping a state-dependent matrix positive definite. Matrix control barrier functions (MCBFs) enforce such requirements with a semidefinite program that minimally modifies a nominal control input. The MCBF constraint bounds how fast the safety margin, the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix, may decay. Yet a fixed decay rule is conservative, rejecting safe controls that drive the state quickly toward, but never across, the boundary of the safe set. Scalar optimal decay (SOD) addresses this issue by scaling the decay term by a scalar weight that is optimized together with the control. For scalar barrier functions, SOD then rejects a control at the boundary only if the control would decrease the margin. For MCBFs, however, SOD can reject controls that leave the margin unchanged, and near the safety boundary SOD accepts such controls only at a high cost. We introduce matrix optimal decay (MOD), which replaces the scalar weight with a matrix multiplier while keeping the semidefinite program convex. MOD is provably sound and complete, certifying at the boundary exactly the controls that do not decrease the margin. If some control can strictly increase the margin at every boundary point, the MOD-MCBF filtered controller is continuous and renders the safe set forward invariant. We also add an optional recovery condition that drives the system toward the safe set after a violation without affecting soundness or completeness. On a planar two-link arm avoiding singularities, MOD-MCBF certifies safe motions that both a fixed decay rule and SOD reject, and tracks an end-effector target more closely than SOD.

arxiv.title: Enforcing a Strict Safety Margin in LLM Text Generation via Barrier Lyapunov Control
arxiv.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed without formal guarantees against toxic text generation. Existing control barrier function (CBF) based safety filters can keep the generation trajectory within a toxicity-free region, but do not enforce a positive distance from its boundary, allowing formally safe trajectories to approach the toxicity threshold arbitrarily closely and leaving little buffer against modelling errors or disturbances. We address this limitation with a Barrier Lyapunov Function (BLF) safety filter that enforces a prescribed clearance margin throughout generation while retaining the continuous-time transformer dynamics, including feedforward layers. The resulting safe input set is a half-space defined by a constraint affine in the control input, and is non-empty under certified surjectivity and classifier-nondegeneracy conditions. For margin-compatible initial conditions we prove that the clearance margin is never violated and that the prescribed clearance is restored exponentially, yielding an explicit clearance floor, and show that, as the margin vanishes, the admissible trajectories satisfy the exponential second-order CBF condition. We further derive an explicitly computable sufficient disturbance budget under which the clearance guarantee degrades gracefully. Simulations on a small transformer illustrate the resulting improvement in safety clearance.

arxiv.title: Safe Unicycle Navigation Among Multiple Obstacles Under Bounded Disturbances: A Learning-Augmented CLF-CBF Approach (Extended Version)
arxiv.abstract: This paper presents a robust control framework for safe navigation of a unicycle robot to a goal among multiple static obstacles under an unknown, time-varying disturbance. The controller solves a single real-time quadratic program (QP) that combines a goal-reaching term with one safety term per obstacle. The goal-reaching term is a cross-track control Lyapunov function built from body-frame tracking errors rather than a bearing angle, which keeps its Lie derivatives bounded everywhere, including the goal. Safety is encoded using robust control barrier functions, one per obstacle, each tightened by a closed-form, state-dependent disturbance bound. When stabilization and safety conflict, a slack variable relaxes only the convergence requirement, so that the safety constraints remain strictly enforced. Whenever the QP is feasible, the robust barrier constraints guarantee forward invariance of every obstacle's safe set under all admissible disturbances. Complementing this safety guarantee, a Lyapunov analysis yields an explicit ultimate bound on the distance to the goal. A learning-augmented variant replaces the fixed objective with a reinforcement-learning reference, which accelerates convergence when multiple constraints are simultaneously active. We further derive the obstacle separation below which the gap between two obstacles becomes too narrow to pass through under the robust constraints. For such gaps, a learned virtual goal for the Lyapunov function steers the robot around the obstacles without compromising safety. Simulations, a Monte Carlo study, and a comparison against a sampled-data robust baseline support the theoretical results.

arxiv.title: Beyond Safe Execution: Safe Online Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving with Value Calibration and Adaptive Guidance
arxiv.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables driving policies to adapt to changing deployment conditions, but requires safe exploration throughout training. Safety filtering alone does not ensure stable policy improvement or reduced dependence on corrections. We propose Safe Online Adaptive Refinement (SOAR-Flow), a framework for safe and stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized Flow-based driving policies. A control barrier function (CBF)--model predictive control (MPC) filter corrects potentially unsafe actions before execution. To support stable policy updates, we introduce Gaussian-return-aware value calibration based on calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL), using recorded behavior returns and predicted return variability to smooth conservative critic updates and mitigate policy degradation. Paired corrective learning teaches feasible action adjustments, while an intervention-to-go predictor encourages decisions requiring fewer future corrections. Its predictions also regulate guidance strength, allowing recovery supervision to weaken as predicted dependence decreases. Together with gradually reduced calibration regularization, this supports continued task improvement while preserving hard execution constraints. We analyze conditions for safe execution at control steps and diminishing auxiliary learning influences. We evaluate SOAR-Flow in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV). The results demonstrate improved driving performance and reduced reliance on safety corrections during protected online fine-tuning. The demonstration video and project overview are available at https://lzqw.github.io/SOAR-Flow/.

arxiv.title: Constrained Grid-Forming Control for Photovoltaic Systems: A Control Barrier Function Approach
arxiv.abstract: This paper leverages control barrier functions (CBFs) to systematically account for constraints of voltage source converters (VSCs) and photovoltaic (PV) resources in grid-forming (GFM) control. The proposed control combines (unconstrained) dual-port GFM control with control barrier functions (CBFs) to ensure reliable and safe operation of a GFM PV system under grid faults, sudden changes in irradiance, and load perturbations. First, CBFs are used to encode physical and operational limits of the PV system, namely current and voltage limits at its ac and dc terminals. Then, CBFs are used to restrict the dynamics of dual-port GFM control to within the VSC and PV limits during both transient and steady states. To this end, a cost function is defined that encodes trade-offs between forming the ac voltage phase angle/frequency and voltage magnitude under constraints. Then, real-time optimization is used to make the least modification, as measured by the cost function, to the (unconstrained) dual-port GFM control state to remain within the safe set encoded by the CBFs. Finally, the performance of the developed constrained GFM control is evaluated through EMT simulations in MATLAB/Simulink.

arxiv.title: Filtering for Liveness: Recurrence via Backup Reachability Control Barrier Functions
arxiv.abstract: Liveness requires a dynamical system to repeatedly accomplish a desired objective over time. In this work, we consider a particular form of liveness known as recurrence, which requires the closed-loop trajectory to regularly revisit a prescribed set, with no more than a specified amount of time between visits. Inspired by the control barrier function (CBF) safety-filter paradigm, we develop a controller-filtering framework that makes adjustments to a nominal controller only when necessary to guarantee recurrence. Unlike conventional CBF methods, which enforce set forward invariance, our framework allows the trajectory to leave the set while guaranteeing its timely return. To achieve this, our framework combines two components: a backup reachability CBF that preserves the ability to return to the prescribed set within the allowable time, and a timing-based mechanism that invokes a reaching controller only when the nominal behavior would otherwise fail to meet the return-time requirement. The resulting framework guarantees recurrence while preserving the nominal behavior when possible, enabling control objectives that require temporary excursions from the set, such as traversal between disjoint regions. Our method is successfully utilized in a drone racing example with a recurrence constraint on beacon visibility.

arxiv.title: Safety-Aware Dimension Selection for Reduced-Order Model Predictive Control
arxiv.abstract: Model reduction can substantially reduce the computational burden of model predictive control (MPC) for high-dimensional systems, but a reduced dimension chosen for performance may be insufficient for safety-critical operation. This paper introduces a safety-aware dimension-selection framework in which the prediction model adapts to the order of the model required to maintain a certified finite-horizon safety condition. Dynamic active subspaces provide a performance-oriented ordering of reduced coordinates, while finite-horizon error bounds robustly enforce discrete-time control barrier function constraints. The controller selects the smallest prediction order for which the resulting safety-critical MPC problem remains feasible. We establish full-order horizon safety, recursive feasibility, and closed-loop invariance of the safe set under the proposed reduced-order formulation. The proposed approach therefore adapts the prediction complexity to safety requirements, avoiding unnecessary high-dimensional prediction during benign operation.

arxiv.title: Joint-Feasibility Margin Feedback for Bounded-Input Second-Order Control Barrier Functions
arxiv.abstract: Multiple second-order control barrier function constraints can exhaust their common control authority under bounded acceleration, even when the current state remains feasible. We define a signed local joint-feasibility margin whose sign exactly identifies whether the current barrier half-spaces intersect the admissible input set. For unit-scaled distance constraints, it has acceleration units and a support-function dual that identifies weighted constraint conflicts. We predict the margin one sample ahead for nine task-directed candidates, selecting either the least-deviating candidate that attains a desired margin or the candidate with the largest predicted margin before solving the same hard HOCBF quadratic program. A controlled one-step case shows that, at the state predicted under the hard-QP command, two constraints remain individually feasible but become jointly infeasible, whereas the margin-feedback controller retains a positive next margin. Separately, across 20 paired initial conditions, the margin-feedback controller retains the hard-QP command in a low-pressure task and acts at positive margin in a critical task before the hard-QP problem becomes infeasible; its trajectories remain feasible at that time and complete the task. Source code is publicly available. https://github.com/xirhxq/cbf/tree/robio2026-preventive-regulation

arxiv.title: Safeguarding Intelligent Power Dispatch:A Performance-Equivalent-Model-Based Safety-Critical Control Method for DC Microgrids
arxiv.abstract: Intelligent power dispatch is enabling fast and self-adaptive decision-making in microgrids, yet its deployment in real-world industry remains limited due to unresolved safety concerns. Existing safety-preserving approaches typically rely on an accurate characterization of the feasible operating region, which is impossible to obtain under uncertain and heterogeneous system dynamics. Moreover, even a dispatch command verified as feasible at a discrete setpoint may become unsafe during its continuous physical execution. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a safety-aware dispatch adjustment framework that uses performance-equivalent modeling of closed-loop systems (PEM-CLS) and embeds high-order control barrier functions and control Lyapunov functions within a quadratic programming formulation (HOCBF-CLF-QP). PEM-CLS captures EMS-required power-regulation dynamics solely from port-level responses, without requiring internal subsystem models, parameters, or controller information. Its modeling error is analytically characterized and explicitly bounded, enabling requirement-oriented dynamic abstraction for safety-critical control. Based on these PEMs, the HOCBF-CLF-QP safety controller coordinates heterogeneous transient power responses and corrects unsafe EMS commands to maintain dynamic safety during command execution. Four deliberately constructed extreme stress-test scenarios are used to expose conflicts between nominal EMS commands and physical safety. Without intervention, the DC-bus voltage violates its safety limit in all four cases, whereas the proposed framework maintains QP feasibility and limits the voltage deviation. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides an algorithm-agnostic safety execution layer for intelligent power dispatch without requiring an exact feasible-region model or detailed internal information of lower-level devices.

arxiv.title: Learning Reachability-Based Safety Representations for Real-Time Robot Navigation in Unknown and Dynamic Environments
arxiv.abstract: Safe robot navigation in unknown, dynamic environments requires more than geometric collision checking: a robot still far from an obstacle may be unable to avoid it because of its speed, orientation, or the obstacle's motion. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis captures this in a value function whose sign separates states that admit a safe continuation from those where collision is unavoidable, but computing it online for every newly observed environment is too expensive. This dissertation trains neural implicit representations offline on reachability solutions to give optimization-based controllers this information in real time. Since the value function never exceeds the constraint, it equals a directly computed constraint, such as a signed distance, minus a nonnegative dynamics correction. Learning only this correction keeps represented obstacles outside the predicted safe set despite approximation errors. The first two of five methods use the learned function as a terminal constraint in model predictive control, for static local environments and predicted obstacle motion. The next two use it as a barrier candidate in control barrier function safety filters, for static environments and, through pairwise barriers in relative coordinates, for a varying number of moving obstacles. Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show better collision avoidance than geometric and hand-designed baselines, especially for short horizons and moving obstacles. The fifth method replaces the grid-based offline solver, which limits the first four to low-dimensional models. For control-affine dynamics with polytopic inputs, the HJ Hamiltonian is maximized at a vertex, so a parallelizable tree search over vertex inputs can generate training labels. With a loss from the HJ variational inequality, these labels yield barrier candidates for systems with up to 13 states.

arxiv.title: Imitation Learning of Avoidance Modes for Efficient Multimodal Model Predictive Control
arxiv.abstract: Multimodal model predictive control (MM-MPC) avoids local minima among moving obstacles by solving one optimal control problem (OCP) per combination of avoidance sides, so its computational cost grows exponentially with the number of decision-critical obstacles. We propose SideNet-MPC, which replaces this enumeration with a mode decision learned by imitating MM-MPC as an expert. A graph neural network is trained to predict the expert's minimum-cost mode, one avoidance side per obstacle. Its edges encode, for each obstacle pair, the gap predicted for the moment the vehicle first reaches either obstacle, so a neighbor that blocks a preferred passage can reverse the proposed side. The expert's selection rule compares its minimum-cost mode with the previously executed mode; SideNet-MPC keeps this rule and substitutes the network proposal for the minimum-cost mode. Hence at most two OCPs are solved per control period, and every applied input still comes from an OCP with control barrier function constraints rather than from the network. In $100$ seed-matched closed-loop Monte Carlo runs of mixed traffic, SideNet-MPC reaches $93\%$ of the expert's success rate and needs \SI{18.6}{ms} per control period on a single thread, 48\% less than the expert's \SI{35.5}{ms} on sixteen parallel threads. In a controlled gap sweep, its proposed side reverses in the same gap interval as the expert's, whereas proposers without pairwise edges, trained on the same data, never reverse and all deadlock at the blocked gates of a deterministic scene.

arxiv.title: Jacobian State Augmented Viable Kinematic Safety Filter
arxiv.abstract: Safety Filters (SF) are leveraged to design certifiably safe controllers, which ensures forward invariance on a defined safe set when the filter is feasible. Predictive Safety Filters (PSF) embed these constraints to a closed-loop model-based optimization method to improve constraint satisfaction, and reduce feasibility loss caused by myopic, one-step filtering. Related viability-based methods emphasize approximating a viability kernel which ensures admissible control for all future time, but requires significant computational expense. This work introduces a Jacobian-based kinematic safety filter leveraging an augmented state variable with task-space velocity and filters task-space acceleration to preserve the feasibility of a low-level filter while enforcing joint position and velocity. The proposed method introduces a nested Quadratic Program (QP) formulation, defines a conservative inner approximation of viability envelope and computes a viable planner online. The method is validated in a simplified 2R planar manipulator simulation environment and shows significant improvement compared to a baseline Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (CBF-QP) based filter. The experiments highlights the improvements in terms of computation time compared to traditional PSF and Reference Governor approach while also showing significant reduction in feasibility violations. Lastly, a simplified demonstration on a simulated 6-DoF manipulator highlights the potential scalability of the method to higher degree-of-freedom setups.

arxiv.title: Barrier-Constrained Guidance For Real-time Asynchronous VLA Execution
arxiv.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative and within-chunk future action flexibility,. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.

arxiv.title: Safety-Critical Quadrotor Navigation Using Fourth-Order Control Barrier Functions with Full Nonlinear Quadrotor Dynamics
arxiv.abstract: Safety-critical quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments typically relies on hierarchical architectures in which a high-level safety filter modifies position references that are then tracked by a separate attitude controller. However, this separation can create a mismatch between translational safety objectives and attitude evolution. To address this gap, we propose a safety controller based on fourth-order control barrier functions (CBFs) that explicitly incorporates the full nonlinear quadrotor dynamics, including attitude dynamics and torque-level actuation. Furthermore, we apply the integral high-order CBF technique to resolve the mixed-relative degree issue in the derived constraint formulation. The resulting formulation enforces obstacle-avoidance constraints while optimizing control torques, granting the safety layer direct authority over attitude behavior and eliminating the hierarchical disconnect inherent in reference-tracking safety filters. We validate the approaches in both high-fidelity simulation and real-world flight experiments, demonstrating reliable constraint satisfaction and successful obstacle avoidance. These results suggest that torque-level high-order CBFs provide a practical pathway to provably safer quadrotor navigation under full rigid-body dynamics.

arxiv.title: Convex Safety Filtering via Spectral Selection for Nonconvex Safe Sets
arxiv.abstract: The discrete-time control barrier function condition for a safe set that is a union of convex sets is nonconvex in the control input. For safe sets defined by a matrix concave function through the number of its nonnegative eigenvalues, this paper shows that the set is a union of convex sets, and that the nonconvexity arises because at least one member of the union must hold, not every member. Selecting eigenvectors of the matrix function at the current state yields a convex input constraint that acts only on the eigenvalues determining membership in the set. This constraint is implied by the matrix-wide condition of prior work, and it guarantees a geometric lower bound on each of those eigenvalues along closed-loop trajectories. A double-integrator simulation with a polytope obstacle and a spectrahedron obstacle compares the proposed filter with the matrix-wide condition.

arxiv.title: Constructive Safety-Critical Control for a Class of Underactuated Systems: A Hierarchical Approach
arxiv.abstract: Underactuated systems with nontrivial geometry are abundant in practical robotic problems. However, little is known about constructive safety-critical control design in the presence of underactuation. In this work, we provide a constructive framework for synthesizing safe control architectures and control barrier functions for a class of quadrotor-like underactuated systems. By studying the geometry of their underactuation, we characterize when these systems have natural layered architectures useful for safety-critical control design. Using these architectures, we devise a constructive, hierarchical CBF synthesis procedure and provide conditions under which it succeeds.

arxiv.title: Compute-Constrained Safety Filters with Neuromorphic Event Triggering
arxiv.abstract: Safety filters that rely on control barrier function (CBF) quadratic programs (QPs) are typically analyzed under the assumption that the QP is solved instantaneously, although nonzero computation time can render a computed input unsafe by the time it is applied. This paper develops a dual leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) event-triggered safety filter for linear systems that accounts for this delay. Two LIF states monitor a shifted CBF residual and the deviation of the held input from the nominal feedback law. A computation is initiated when either LIF state reaches its threshold; the previous input remains applied until the prescribed application time, and any solution returned earlier is stored until then. A closed-form charging profile relates the safety-LIF threshold to residual-growth bounds, ensuring sufficient residual margin over the application delay. Under the stated assumptions, the resulting hybrid system guarantees forward invariance, completeness, and non-Zeno execution, with positive lower bounds on computation-initiation and input-application times. A spacecraft terminal-approach simulation demonstrates safety with fewer optimizer calls than a delay-tightened periodic filter.

arxiv.title: Safe Control of Semi-Explicit Differential-Algebraic Systems: Control Barrier Functions with SOS Verification
arxiv.abstract: Differential-algebraic equation (DAE) systems arise in power networks, multibody mechanics, and chemical processes, where algebraic constraints couple dynamic and algebraic states. Standard control barrier function (CBF) methods, designed for ordinary differential equations, fail for DAE systems because the algebraic constraints impose compatibility requirements that may render safety filters infeasible. This paper develops a safety-critical control framework for semi-explicit DAE systems using CBFs that consider compatibility with the algebraic constraints, termed DAE-aware CBFs. We construct projected vector fields on the constraint manifold to account for the hidden dynamics, while ensuring compatibility conditions that keep the algebraic constraints satisfied. We then present sum of squares (SOS) verification conditions that certify both correctness and feasibility of the resulting DAE-aware CBF. The framework is validated on power system case studies.

arxiv.title: HULK: Learning Whole-Body Forceful Loco-Manipulation for Humanoids
arxiv.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation of large, heavy objects demands forceful interaction across the entire body. However, such payloads shift a humanoid's center of mass and impose sustained loads across the upper body, challenging balance and command tracking. We present HULK, a whole-body control framework for forceful loco-manipulation. Using model predictive control (MPC) to guide reinforcement learning with predictions of the loaded dynamics, we train two teachers: one tracks arm motions under wrist forces, and the other locomotes while holding large objects against the body. A capture-point control barrier function augments the wrist-force teacher during training to improve balance under load. We distill both teachers into a single policy. Evaluation spans simulation and the Unitree G1. In simulation, the teacher with the barrier function achieves the lowest forward and lateral velocity tracking errors at 10 kg per arm among evaluated controllers and reduces aggregate divergent component of motion (DCM) excursion magnitude by 35.7% relative to MPC-guided reinforcement learning alone. Our wrist-force teacher withstands torso push disturbances of up to 130 N.

arxiv.title: LBA-CBF: Rapidly Adaptive Safety Filters via Parallel Dynamics Inference
arxiv.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) certify commands through an assumed dynamics model, so an abrupt, unmeasured regime change can undermine the certificate exactly when safety matters most. We present Look-Back Adaptive Control Barrier Functions (LBA-CBF), which rank a finite bank of candidate dynamics by recent prediction error over a short look-back window and enforce the high-order CBF condition against every model within a tolerance of the best, spanning best-fit adaptation to full-bank robust filtering. The dynamics may depend nonlinearly on the unknown parameters, and no switching model or continuously parameterized estimator is required. We prove that any feasible filtered input satisfies the true CBF condition whenever a safety-representative candidate is retained. In quadrotor simulation with abrupt wind reversals and an unknown payload, LBA-CBF is safe and reaches the goal from all random initial conditions, matching an oracle, while adaptive and robust baselines achieve 0-88% success. Banks of up to 250,000 models run inside the control loop, and Crazyflie 2.1 and F1TENTH experiments demonstrate adaptation to wind, payload release, and varying tire-road friction. Code, videos, and project details are available at: https://lla-control.github.io

arxiv.title: Safe Multi-Robot Collaborative Transport Using Density Functions
arxiv.abstract: This paper presents a hierarchical density-based model predictive control framework for safe collaborative manipulation by multiple quadrupedal robots. The framework enables a team of robots to push a shared object to a desired pose using only the initial and goal poses, without requiring a precomputed reference trajectory. A centralized box-level MPC optimizes contact forces while enforcing a control-density constraint for goal convergence and obstacle avoidance. Each robot then solves its own distributed robot-level whole-body MPC, under a stated shared-information assumption, to track its moving contact location while accounting for static obstacles and the time-varying positions of neighboring robots. The approach is evaluated in MuJoCo using whole-body contact dynamics for two and three Unitree Go2 quadrupeds collaboratively pushing rigid objects through narrow passages. Comparisons with matched Control Barrier Function and RRT* based tracking baselines demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed density-based formulation for push-only, force- and torque-coupled manipulation tasks. Implementation videos are available at https://jaggu2606.github.io/go2-density-mpc-pushing/

arxiv.title: SC3BF: Shifted Collision Cone Control Barrier Function for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
arxiv.abstract: The collision cone used by velocity-space control barrier functions is conservative: it rejects every relative velocity aimed into an obstacle, however slow. We propose the \emph{shifted collision-cone CBF} (SC3BF), which adds a state-dependent \emph{allowance} to the cone condition, so the robot may approach the obstacle at a rate that grows with distance and with its own speed. SC3BF is enforced by an ordinary quadratic program, and its safe set is forward invariant under bounded inputs without a minimum forward speed or a clearance margin. We prove that a nonzero allowance preserving safety always exists, and derive one in closed form. Against three velocity-space baselines on a kinematic bicycle among up to $100$ moving obstacles, SC3BF reaches the goal more often and modifies the nominal input less than half as much.

arxiv.title: Context-Conditioned Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability for Adaptive Safety Filtering
arxiv.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi reachability constructs safety certificates for specified dynamics and safety constraints, tying each certificate to the deployment context for which it is synthesized. We ask whether a single certificate can instead represent a family of context-dependent safety problems and be queried across deployment conditions without re-synthesis. We learn a backward reachable tube for an eight-state vehicle model conditioned on local boundary geometry, friction coefficient, and adversarial disturbance scale. Geometry enters through an ego-frame boundary observation that defines the local containment constraint, while friction and disturbance scale enter as explicit operating-condition variables. This allows the same value function to be queried across friction coefficients from 0.4 to 2.0 and on geometries absent from synthesis. On 11 held-out evaluation geometries, the certificate maintains containment across the full tested friction range, including simultaneous geometry and grip shifts, while remaining within 1.2 percentage points in intervention rate and 0.09 m/s in speed of certificates re-synthesized with knowledge of the test geometry. We then deploy the certificate as a sampled discrete-time control barrier function filter on a full-scale vehicle near the handling limit. Lateral containment holds in every hardware session under both adversarial driving and autonomous racing, with 99th-percentile acceleration magnitude reaching 0.99 g. Across three certificates evaluated under a fixed autonomous racing controller, lap time varies by only 3.1%, demonstrating that a context-conditioned reachability certificate can transfer to deployment geometries absent from synthesis with modest performance cost.

arxiv.title: Exact-Safe MPPI: Safety-Aware Sampling with Nonsmooth Control Barrier Functions
arxiv.abstract: Model predictive path integral (MPPI) control plans actions by sampling and evaluating trajectories, but standard MPPI does not guarantee safety. Incorporating control barrier function (CBF) filters into each rollout allows the planner to account for safety corrections. However, combining multiple CBFs through a soft-minimum approximation can exclude states that satisfy the original safety constraints, restricting the trajectories available to the planner. This paper proposes Exact-Safe MPPI, which uses the exact minimum of multiple barrier functions and applies a CBF-based quadratic program during both planning and control execution. To handle nondifferentiability where multiple barriers attain the minimum, the filter simultaneously enforces the CBF conditions for all $δ$-active barriers, whose values lie within a prescribed tolerance $δ>0$ of the minimum. Under suitable feasibility and regularity assumptions, we establish forward invariance of the certified safe set without the shrinkage introduced by soft-minimum smoothing. We also characterize the state-dependent approximation gap and explain how multiple barriers with values at or near the minimum increase this shrinkage. Furthermore, we show that increasing the number of MPPI samples cannot recover trajectories excluded by the soft-minimum filter. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in a navigation task requiring passage through a narrow gap between two obstacles. Video demonstrations are available at https://github.com/lc-lab25/Exact-Safe-MPPI .

arxiv.title: Vector Field Following for Quadrotors via Reduced Attitude Representations with Applications to Safety-Critical Control
arxiv.abstract: Vector field tracking for quadrotors provides a systematic framework for specifying complex behaviors at the translational level and transferring them to the full vehicle dynamics. Objectives such as safety, for example, can be encoded into a low-dimensional vector field, which is then embedded into the full dynamics through appropriate tracking conditions. The development of such tracking controllers for quadrotors can be facilitated by the fact that their translational dynamics depend only on the thrust direction and are independent of the vehicle's heading. Thus, reduced-attitude representations, leveraging the geometry of the unit sphere, provide a natural framework for vector field tracking on quadrotors. In this work, we propose two vector field tracking controllers for quadrotors using reduced-attitude representations based on dynamic extension and geometric control, respectively. Next, we illustrate how safety can be encoded into the desired vector field using control barrier functions and enforced for the full system. The effectiveness of the proposed approaches is demonstrated via simulations and experimental flight tests.

arxiv.title: Safe Receding-Horizon Control of Fixed-Wing Aircraft Using Constrained Approximate Dynamic Programming
arxiv.abstract: We present a receding-horizon optimal control for fixed-wing aircraft subject to state constraints. These constraints include operational constraints such as altitude, geofencing, and obstacle avoidance, as well as bounds on flight-path angle, roll angle, and airspeed. The state constraints are composed into a single soft-minimum control barrier function (CBF). We use this composite CBF in a constrained-approximate dynamic program to obtain a sequence of analytic closed-form control functions that approximately minimize a quadratic finite-horizon integral cost subject to the CBF constraint. The resulting receding-horizon control is non-myopic in the sense that it approximately optimizes the integral cost while satisfying the state constraint at all times along the entire prediction horizon. We demonstrate constraint satisfaction and performance in simulations of a fixed-wing aircraft navigating an obstacle-filled airspace under wind uncertainty. We also compare this receding-horizon control with 2 other methods.

arxiv.title: Neural Barriers: An Online Certifiable Learning-enhanced Adaptive High Order Safety Critical Control
arxiv.abstract: Control barrier functions are an effective model-based tool to formally certify the safety of a system. However, transferring their theoretical guarantees to real-world robotics systems requires high model fidelity. For example, payloads or wind disturbances can cause significant model perturbations to an aerial vehicle, leading to safety compromises. In this work, we propose a certifiable online learning-enhanced robust adaptive control barrier function, which adapts to disturbances using a Neural ODE and quantifies its adaptation uncertainty with conformal prediction. Our approach guarantees safety at all time under unknown time-varying model disturbances. It adopts a conservative strategy when the adaptation uncertainty is high; and efficiently adapts to reduce controller conservativeness as it receives more data. Our approach provides a provable safety guarantee with a probability bound under suitable Lipschitz smoothness assumptions on the underlying model and trajectory. These results demonstrate the potential of our method as a practical safety controller for robotics system operating under model perturbations.

arxiv.title: Backup Control Barrier Functions with Memory for Online Set Expansion
arxiv.abstract: Backup control barrier functions (bCBFs) construct implicit safe sets for nonlinear systems with bounded inputs using finite-horizon predictions under a backup controller. As in model predictive control, an invariant backup set serves as a terminal set that guarantees safe continuation beyond the prediction horizon. However, reaching a small terminal set may require long prediction horizons, increasing the cost of online prediction. In this paper, we introduce an online construction that builds a certified region from sets stored along backup trajectories while keeping the prediction horizon fixed. The method stores finite collections of balls and connects each newly certified collection to the backup set or to previously stored balls. We derive conditions that guarantee forward invariance of the union of these balls and the backup set under a fixed backup controller. These conditions also ensure that every stored state reaches the backup set in finite time. The resulting union serves as an enlarged terminal set, allowing safety to be certified with shorter prediction horizons. We formulate a feasible quadratic program for safe control and prove that safety is preserved as additional certified collections are stored online. Simulations on a quadrotor demonstrate safe task completion with a shorter prediction horizon than the standard bCBF.
